source.title: The difference between squat jump and countermovement jump in 770 male and female participants from different sports

paper.citation: Kozinc Ž., Žitnik J., Smajla D., Šarabon N. The difference between squat jump and countermovement jump in 770 male and female participants from different sports. European Journal of Sport Science. 2022;22(7):985-993. doi:10.1080/17461391.2021.1936654.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Do athlete groups with better squat-jump and countermovement-jump performance also show a larger relative difference between those jumps, and how do sport and sex relate to the three outcomes? The convenience sample included 712 competitive athletes and 58 physically active physical-education students across basketball, dance, karate, long-distance running, soccer, speed skating, tennis, short-distance running, and volleyball. Mean subgroup ages ranged from 15.7 to 36.3 years; soccer and volleyball included only males, and subgroup sizes were highly unequal. This was a cross-sectional, single-session study. After a standardized warm-up and familiarization, participants completed randomized squat-jump and countermovement-jump conditions with three recorded trials each, hands on hips, and approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion.
paper.tldr: Sport and sex were associated with squat-jump and countermovement-jump height, with short-distance runners producing the highest mean heights and long-distance runners generally the lowest; these group comparisons describe this sample rather than causal sport effects. Only 48.4% of participants had a countermovement jump clearly higher than their squat jump; 17.5% jumped higher in the squat jump, and 34.0% had a between-jump difference smaller than the cited typical inter-repetition error of 1.51 cm. Do not label a large countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference as automatically “good,” or prescribe training from that difference alone.
paper.methods: This was a cross-sectional, single-session study. After a standardized warm-up and familiarization, participants completed randomized squat-jump and countermovement-jump conditions with three recorded trials each, hands on hips, and approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion. Jump height was derived from force-platform impulse and takeoff velocity; the best trial was retained, and the relative difference was calculated as (CMJ minus SJ) divided by SJ times 100. Two-way ANOVA examined sport and sex effects, with correlations used for secondary associations.
paper.findings: Sport and sex were associated with squat-jump and countermovement-jump height, with short-distance runners producing the highest mean heights and long-distance runners generally the lowest; these group comparisons describe this sample rather than causal sport effects. Only 48.4% of participants had a countermovement jump clearly higher than their squat jump; 17.5% jumped higher in the squat jump, and 34.0% had a between-jump difference smaller than the cited typical inter-repetition error of 1.51 cm. Physical-education students showed the largest relative jump difference despite not being the highest-performing jump group, whereas most athlete groups had broadly similar values. The relative difference was moderately associated with countermovement-jump height across the full sample (r = 0.41) but was not associated with squat-jump height (r = 0.03); this association does not identify the mechanism producing the difference. Sport-group patterns differed depending on whether the outcome was jump height, peak power, or push-off time, undermining a single universal interpretation of the countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference. The authors concluded that a larger difference is not necessarily better and may reflect several factors, including muscle-tendon slack, rate-of-force-development capability, technique, or task familiarity rather than only superior stretch-shortening-cycle use.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot establish why groups differed or how training changes the metric. Recruitment was by convenience; subgroup ages, sizes, sex representation, and training backgrounds were unbalanced, with very small speed-skating and sprint subgroups and no women in soccer or volleyball. Within-group variability was substantial, the best trial rather than an average was analyzed, and the composite difference inherits error from both jump tests. No collegiate American football players were studied, so direct norm transfer is inappropriate. The broad measurement lesson is applicable, but football-specific reference values and longitudinal sensitivity require local validation.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not label a large countermovement-jump versus squat-jump difference as automatically “good,” or prescribe training from that difference alone. Examine the two component jumps, their force-time characteristics, technique quality, reliability, and change relative to the athlete’s own typical error. In collegiate American football, use position- and athlete-specific longitudinal baselines and pair any difference score with direct measures relevant to the question, such as jump height, impulse, strategy, or force-velocity characteristics. This paper supports cautious interpretation; it does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a training algorithm.

paper.rtp: The paper did not validate a rehabilitation or return-to-sport decision rule. Its findings may inform supporting training or monitoring during reconditioning, but it provides no standalone clearance threshold or progression criterion.
